574.t: Dance halls and pavilions in Thibodaux
574.s: Where bands played, the fireground and Coxwood pavilions, segregation of the venues and the size of the town.
574.q: Yeah, open on the floor, all around on the side. Get cold, you just set the windows down. I had another place up there, but this open alley, you could call it Cox.

574.t: Society banquet jobs and prohibition near-beer
574.s: Anniversary banquets at society halls paid two dollars; dinner of gumbo and stew, near-beer, playing until five.
574.q: No, we used to be in the hall. Oh, the hall. Yeah. All everyone operated was in the hall. Like a dance hall. Yeah, like the cooperators, perseverance, new hall, sometimes the economy. That's what he, that's them old societies. Yeah. That's what they called the anniversary. They called them bonquets.

248.t: What dances at St. Catharines Hall were like
248.s: Dances were occasional, ticketed, with soft drinks and sandwiches but no liquor, under Father Moe; the bands played Dixieland and occasionally hymns.
248.ch: Opening, St. Catharines Hall and the Odd Fellows
248.q: No, once a week like that, once a month like that. Oh, yeah. The Catholic place, you know. Oh, yeah. And, uh, they used to give, uh,

430.s: Societies gave Monday afternoon banquets at halls, each with a band.
430.q: Yeah. You see, and then the other thing, on a Monday, they're all, all the societies, they always gave, they gave their banquets on a Monday. You see, like, maybe, yes, so they were, well, for instance, it was Monday. Well, you see, they had a banquet maybe at Poison Furnace Hall, Economy Hall, and…

899.s: Dances were on Sunday nights from 8 to 3 and society banquets on Monday afternoons, with food and drink funded by the society.
899.q: Yeah, it was a big night, but during them time it was, I don't know, a regular tradition of giving a dance on a Sunday night.

1000.t: Banquets, weddings and few dances; no place for Dixieland now
1000.s: Small halls hosted banquets and weddings rather than balls; today Dixieland bands play in the country, such as a Shell Beach job with Doc.
1000.q: Yeah, different, but that ball never did take much, because the copyright is in the Hoops Hall, they used to call it. The Hoops Hall, that was it. They called it the copyright, but it's the Hoops Hall. They called it the Hoops Hall, and then they ate, they called it the copyright. But the old…

1.t: Lawn parties and dance halls of the Seventh Ward
1.s: He describes lawn parties and tries with the interviewer to locate halls by ward.
1.ch: Boyhood scene: halls and dance music
1.q: That's my best ministry. Oh, yeah. But the way it happened, there's another hall, like, the night was, it was an independent hall, and then the, the Grand Union Hall. I don't know about it. I know that wasn't 6th Ward, too. There's a lot of halls I've collected in my material that nobody's ever…

571.t: First hearing Bunk, and society anniversary banquets
571.s: George recalls hearing Bunk in his twenties around New Orleans halls and describes how benevolent societies held banquets with food, beer and a band.
571.ch: Mandeville, Bunk Johnson and society banquets
571.q: Well, the first time I heard Bunk was in his twenties. That's the first time I heard Bunk when Bunk was a younger man. I heard Bunk in New Orleans too. I heard Bunk here on Parades. I heard Bunk at Banquets. You know, we called Bunk kids. We called them Bunk kids at the Hopes Hall. I heard him at…

601.t: Old Man Solace's grocery, the little hall and the Catholic church on Patterson Street
601.s: Asked about parks and lawn parties, Martin describes a small place at old man Solace's grocery on Patterson Street, with stables and a church next door, where people danced.
601.q: Well, you take... They used to have a little place, Old Man Solace there. Oh, that's at the Cudolph, isn't it? No. Right there in the Lisey. That's where that's the Lisey there, yeah. Old Man Solace. Yeah, well... They all used to play that. Yeah, that's where Little Hall was. Little Hall. When you…

873.t: Who sponsored dances and parades, and playing in church
873.s: Community clubs, dance halls and the Benevolent Society paid for dances and parades; Lawrence played midnight mass.
873.q: Well, we had a community club at Notchua. It was a club they had in response to dancing. And Moray, Louis Moray, he had a dancing place. Every Sunday he had a dance.

569.t: Miss Coles's lawn parties and dance halls
569.s: He describes Miss Coles's lawn parties and dance hall, plus St. Elizabeth and St. Dominic Halls, with prices, food and hours.
569.q: Well it was a dance hall, you know, that first was lawn parties, years ago, and then she made a dance hall. She did? Yeah, regular big dance hall. Did she build it out in their yard? Build it, build it in that big vacant place where we used to have the, she used to have the lawn parties. Where was…

404.t: Artesian and Economy Hall societies and their banquets
404.s: How benevolent societies at Artesian and Economy Halls gave banquets, with banquet funds from the treasury.
404.q: Well, that was different. They had societies. They had the ladies belong to that. That's how they started to have them in banquets. Yeah, and they had a burial too. Yeah, yeah, they had... It was a regular society.

635.t: The 'bunk cave' banquets with free food and wine
635.s: The banquet tradition, with free food and drink, as at Perseverance Hall; the last one played with Manuel around 1909-10.
635.q: Yeah, we played a bunk cave. The last bunk cave we played together, Manuel. It was at the Perseverance Hall on Vero Street with George and Freddie Kemper that finished the leave. That was around 99, was it? Yeah. 99 or 1910. Around 99. I think it was nine.

886.s: Brass bands once played banquets, as with Wooden Joe; they are now called banquets.
886.q: That's right. You live in the hall now, that period of bonquet. That's the new hall you call it. Down on the... On the island of the near on east. Mm-hmm. The island of the near on east. Of course, there's a very hard on the period of bonquet. But you don't have that no more. Long time.

801.s: Economy Hall-type Monday dances, and society banquets with free food, ham and beer where Eddie got friends in.
801.q: I played a couple of them. Yeah, they call them bonquets. I played a couple of them night ones. There were very few night ones there in my head.

832.s: Asked about dances across the lake, Foster says there were dances at the Southern Dollars Hall in Mandeville.
832.q: Yeah, they had dances over there. They had the Southern Dollars Hall, I said that, but they had dances. And this same boy, I'll speak about, I will tell you a little later about that, what it be a tea, you know. Yeah. That's where he used to come and play. That's in Mandelville.

128.t: Economy Hall dances and society banquets
128.s: Bands at Economy Hall and the social-club banquets where food and music were plentiful.
128.ch: Country bands, trombone and city life
128.q: what a team Sam Morgan, Kid Renny, all different bands you understand? Butt Carry on, Kid Punch all different bands every Sunday night there was a dance on Monday was a dance and sometime through the week especially through the week on Thursday or Friday or Wednesday they had bands they had bonques…

306.t: What the dance halls were like: admission, deposits, manners and wine
306.s: Edna describes society balls, how bands were paid a deposit, respectable slow dancing, intermissions and Chris's wine.
306.q: Well, the dance hall is big and wide and they have little benches upside the wall. All around. In the kitchen they have, in the back they have something like a room with drinks and that. And the music be up on the stand and all the lights is on and you get up and dance.

8.t: Kitchen Mechanics Night at Aaron's Hall
8.s: The band gave its own Thursday dance for domestic servants on their night off.
8.q: (Unintelligible). They used to every Thursday, the band would give their own dance at AARON'S HALL. That's the night
